rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient spanning nearly the full solvent-strength range at mid temperature to reveal overall retention spread, missing late eluters, and clustering. This gives a balanced first map of the mixture for subsequent optimization.

All 10 compounds are already baseline resolved, so the opportunity is to reduce analysis time while preserving the tightest mid-run separations. A moderately steeper full-range gradient should test how much runtime can be cut before the 6-8 region becomes limiting.

The 14 min gradient is very fast but compresses the critical 6/7 pair too much, so a small increase in gradient time should restore that separation while likely keeping the run in the zero time-penalty region. This is a local refinement around the current best conditions.

The optimum appears near the 14 min full-range gradient, limited by the 6/7 pair. Lowering temperature should selectively increase retention and often improves selectivity enough to open that critical pair while keeping total runtime near the current best.

Lower temperature hurt selectivity by creating a new near-coelution, so test the opposite direction. A modest increase to 45 C may improve the critical mid-cluster selectivity or at least confirm whether 40 C is the local optimum while maintaining very short runtime.

Temperature changes worsened selectivity, so keep 40 C and instead weaken early retention control by raising phi0 slightly while preserving a fast full-strength finish. This should decompress the earliest part of the gradient and may reshuffle spacing in the crowded 5–6 min cluster without adding much time.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved both speed and the score, suggesting the crowded mid-cluster benefits from a shallower effective early gradient. Push phi0 one more step higher to see if the critical 6/7 spacing improves further while staying in the zero time-penalty window.

The best region is around phi0 0.10 and 14 min, but the limiting pair still sits just below ideal. Increasing tG by one step at the improved phi0 should selectively recover enough separation in the crowded cluster, and the score may improve if the time penalty stays very small.

Now that baseline separation is achieved with only a tiny time penalty, probe whether a slightly lower phi1 can fine-tune late-gradient selectivity while keeping all compounds eluting comfortably early. This is a focused selectivity test around the near-optimal method rather than a major change.

The phi1 change only increased run time, so keep the best gradient shape and probe a small temperature increase at the optimal phi0/tG point. This checks whether selectivity at the critical cluster can be maintained or improved enough to offset any slight compression and possibly reveal a still better local optimum.

The current best is very close to ideal, so the main question is whether a slightly longer gradient can retain full resolution with only a negligible extra time penalty. Testing 18 min at the established optimal temperature and phi-range maps the local maximum around the best method.

The local time optimum is clearly near 16 min, so rather than lengthening further, test whether a cooler temperature at the best gradient shape changes selectivity enough to improve the limiting 6/7 pair without a meaningful time penalty. This is the last key local orthogonal probe around the current best point.

Temperature is clearly unfavorable away from 40 C, so keep the best temperature and test a higher phi0 at the successful 16 min gradient. Since phi0 = 0.10 improved over 0.05 and 0.15 at 14 min was still strong, phi0 = 0.20 may further optimize the crowded mid-gradient region while preserving short runtime.

A smaller drop from phi1 0.95 to 0.85 is a tighter selectivity probe than the 0.90 test and may preserve the excellent critical-pair spacing while shifting the overall pattern toward a zero time-penalty optimum. This is one of the few nearby unexplored settings around the current maximum.

The gradient parameters are now well optimized, so the remaining unexplored local axis is a larger temperature increase at the best gradient shape. Although 45 C was worse, a nonmonotonic selectivity change is still possible and this test can decisively rule in or out hotter conditions near the optimum.

The best method may reflect a tradeoff between phi0 and tG, so test whether lowering phi0 while slightly lengthening the gradient can keep the strong 16 min selectivity but reduce the residual time penalty structure. This explores a nearby ridge in method space not yet sampled directly.

At 16 min and 40 C, increasing phi0 to 0.20 kept the method very strong and shortened the run, so one more step higher could move the method onto an even better zero-penalty plateau. This directly tests whether the optimum continues toward higher phi0 or has already turned over.

Very high and low temperatures around the optimum have not been fully excluded, and the selectivity changes are clearly nonlinear. A 30 C test at the best gradient may reveal a different ordering/selectivity regime that improves the critical cluster enough to outweigh a small time increase.

The optimum is tightly centered at 40 C and 16 min, with phi0 between 0.10 and 0.20 performing best, but 0.15 at 16 min remains untested. This fills the key interpolation point and could outperform both neighboring phi0 values if the selectivity maximum lies between them.

You have already reached the maximum CRF, so further runs should map the plateau around the optimum and look for equally scoring but even faster conditions. This tests whether the higher-phi0 region can recover a perfect score at the shorter 14 min gradient.

With a perfect method already found, the most useful remaining experiment is to define the local plateau in gradient time at the optimal phi0. Testing 18 min shows whether the perfect score is robust to a slightly shallower gradient or whether 16 min is a sharp optimum.

With the optimum already found, a useful final local probe is to reduce phi1 slightly at the optimal phi0 and tG to see whether the perfect score extends across a nearby selectivity plateau. This tests the only remaining small orthogonal change around the maximum that has not been sampled at phi0 0.15.

The 0.90 endpoint stayed very close to optimal, so one more small decrease in phi1 will define the edge of the high-scoring plateau at the true optimum phi0/tG. This is the most informative remaining local perturbation around the perfect method.

The optimum in gradient composition is now clear, so use one of the final injections to complete the temperature map exactly at the best phi0/tG point. This confirms whether the perfect score is uniquely tied to 40 C or if a nearby thermal variant can match it.
